newsitem.title: USA: NASA chief defends Russia on global space station.
newsitem.headline: NASA chief defends Russia on global space station.

text.p: NASA chief Dan Goldin on Tuesday defended Russia's commitment to the international space station, but acknowledged that the "day of reckoning" would soon be at hand.

"Everyone knows we have challenges with the Russians," Goldin told members of the House Space and Aeronautics subcommittee. "We want to work with them but they have to live up to the promises they make."

Goldin said he was concerned by last week's announcement in Moscow that money troubles in Russia would delay the launch of the first element of the space station by seven months, which critics allege could jeopardise the $40 billion project.
"We cannot handle much more restructuring ... The day of reckoning is at hand, it takes two to tango," Goldin said.
Under pointed questioning, Goldin said he could not confirm whether the Russian Space Agency had received an expected $100 million infusion of cash by Feb. 28.

Goldin said Russia needs $300 million to keep its commitments for 1997, but could not say what its requirements were for the coming years of space station construction. He noted that until a few months ago, he had no idea how much Russia was spending on its part of the international project.

Representative Dana Rohrabacher, a California Republican who chairs the subcommittee, asked whether Goldin and NASA had considered changing the nature of Russia's participation from full partner -- along with the space agencies of Europe, Japan and Canada -- to subcontractor.
"We're going to do everything possible to continue the current relationship," Goldin said.

Goldin has dispatched an expert team to Moscow from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration to determine whether the Russian cash crunch is severe enough to warrant putting contingency plans for the space station into effect.

In addition to questions about the space station, Goldin faced a grilling from members of Congress over NASA's proposed $13.5 billion budget for fiscal 1998 -- at least one congressman felt it was too low -- the cutting of funds from the space shuttle programme and problems with maintenance at NASA's centres around the country.
